topics: 🌾 Fifty Sela Per Beit Kor — measuring an ancestral field, and what crevices and boulders don't count
💰 A Sela and a Pundeyon Per Year — paid all at once, plus the owner's extra fifth
👨‍👦 Who Redeems Determines Who Keeps It — the owner, his son, another person, or a priest
🤔 Rami bar Ḥama's Dilemma — does a field consecrated less than two years before the Jubilee still go to the priests?
⛪ The Unredeemed Field at the Jubilee — Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Eliezer's three-way dispute

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Valuing and Redeeming an Ancestral Field
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 25a–25b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ שָׂדֵהוּ בִּשְׁעַת הַיּוֹבֵל, נוֹתֵן בְּזֶרַע חוֹמֶר שְׂעוֹרִים חֲמִשִּׁים שֶׁקֶל כָּסֶף
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having established the timing rules around the Jubilee, the daf now works through the mechanics of consecrating and redeeming an ancestral field: how the field is measured (excluding unusable crevices and boulders), how the price is calculated per year remaining until the Jubilee, and — crucially — who is legally able to redeem it in a way that keeps it in the family. A new mishna maps out four different redeemers and four different outcomes, sparking Gemara dilemmas about daughters, wives, and fields consecrated too close to the Jubilee to be redeemed at a discount. The daf ends with a three-way tannaitic dispute over what happens to a field nobody ever redeemed.

slides.title: 🌾 Measuring and Pricing the Field
slides.subtitle: New mishna: the base valuation and its adjustments
rows: 50 sela (shekels) per beit kor — the area needed to sow a kor of barley by hand, average density
Excluded from the measured area (not fit for sowing)
Included — considered mere 'cracks' or 'ridges' of the field itself
Pay a sela and a pundeyon (1/48 of a sela) per remaining year
Must be paid as one lump sum — 'I'll pay year by year' is not accepted
Only the owner adds an extra one-fifth to the payment

slides.title: 👨‍👧 Why 'Another Man' Excludes a Son but Includes a Brother
slides.subtitle: The Gemara mines Leviticus 27:20's phrase for who does NOT trigger transfer to the priests

nodes.content: ❓ 'To another man' (Lev. 27:20) — the field goes to priests only if redeemed by 'another,' not by the owner's son. But is a brother also excluded?
📜 The word 'man' (ish) in the verse already includes a brother — so 'another' must be adding something more specific: it excludes the son

columns.label: Why include the son?
columns.content: He 'stands in his father's place' for two things: designating a Hebrew maidservant, and inheriting a Hebrew slave (who need not go free)

columns.label: Why not the brother?
columns.content: His only comparable role is levirate marriage (yibum) — but yibum applies only when there is no son, proving a son outranks a brother

callout.label: Left open:
callout.text: Can a daughter redeem and preserve the field for her father, like a son? Rabba bar Avuh's dilemma is resolved: no — for inheritance purposes a daughter (where there's a son) is 'like another.' Whether a woman's field is preserved by her husband or by her son remains an unresolved teiku.

slides.title: 💰 New Mishna: Who Redeems Decides Who Keeps It
slides.subtitle: Four scenarios, four different outcomes at the Jubilee

steps.content: 1️⃣ The owner himself redeems it → it never leaves his hands, even at the Jubilee
2️⃣ His son redeems it → it returns to the father (the original owner) at the Jubilee
3️⃣ Another person or relative redeems it, and the owner then redeems it from them → it still goes to the priests at the Jubilee
4️⃣ A priest redeems it and still holds it at the Jubilee → he may NOT keep it as his own; it's divided among all his priestly brethren

slides.title: 🤔 Rami bar Ḥama's Dilemma
slides.subtitle: What if the field was consecrated too close to the Jubilee to be redeemed at a discount?
slides.label: The question:
slides.text: If someone consecrated his ancestral field less than two years before the Jubilee — meaning it can only be redeemed at the full valuation, never at a year-prorated discount — and he never redeemed it, does it still transfer to the priests when the Jubilee arrives? Rav Ḥisda first floats the idea that only a field 'fit for deduction' transfers to the priests (so this one wouldn't), but then reverses himself: the verse's actual condition is simply whether the field was fit for redemption at all — and this field was, just not at a discount. So yes, an unredeemed field consecrated within two years of the Jubilee still goes to the priests.
slides.hebrewSource: אִם לֹא יִגְאַל אֶת הַשָּׂדֶה... וְהָיָה הַשָּׂדֶה בְּצֵאתוֹ בַיּוֹבֵל

slides.title: ⛪ What Happens to a Field No One Ever Redeemed?
slides.subtitle: New mishna: three tanna'im, three outcomes at the Jubilee

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: The priests enter and take the field — but they must pay its value to the Temple treasury. I derive this by verbal analogy ('holy'–'holy') from a consecrated house, which is also redeemed only for payment.

lines.speaker: R' Shimon
lines.text: The priests enter and take it for free — no payment required. My analogy is to the Shavuot lambs, a gift the priests receive gratis, since this field too is 'a gift to the priests.'

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: The priests don't enter at all! It stays with the Temple treasury, called a 'forsaken field,' until the next Jubilee — and again after that, until someone finally redeems it.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Each tanna's verbal analogy is chosen precisely: R' Yehuda compares consecration-for-Temple-upkeep to another Temple-upkeep case (a house), not to an altar-offering; R' Shimon compares a priestly gift to another priestly gift, not to a non-gift like a house.

summary.principle: An ancestral field's redemption price is precisely calculated by beit kor and remaining years, paid as one lump sum; only the owner or his son preserves it within the family at the Jubilee, while redemption by anyone else sends it to the priests — and if no one redeems it at all, its fate is a three-way tannaitic dispute.

flowSteps.content: 🌾 Base valuation: 50 sela per beit kor, minus unusable crevices/boulders ≥10 handbreadths
👨‍👧 'Another man' excludes only a son (who stands in his father's place) from triggering transfer to the priests — not a brother

columns.content: 💰 Owner redeems → keeps it forever; son redeems → returns to father; anyone else → priests
🤔 Even a field consecrated <2 years before Jubilee (no discount) still transfers to priests if unredeemed

flowSteps.content: ⛪ If truly never redeemed: R' Yehuda (priests pay), R' Shimon (priests take free), or R' Eliezer (no one takes it until someone redeems it)
🎓 Key Principle: the Torah tracks precisely who redeems an ancestral field, because that single fact determines whether it stays in the family forever or becomes the priests' gift

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what areas of a consecrated field are excluded from its measurement for valuation purposes?
o: Any rocky area regardless of size
Crevices or boulders that are at least ten handbreadths deep or high, since they are unfit for sowing
Only areas containing water year-round
The entire field if any part is unusable
quiz.e: The mishna excludes crevices ten handbreadths deep or boulders ten handbreadths high from the measured area, since land at that scale of unevenness is not fit for sowing; smaller irregularities are still counted as part of the field.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara conclude that the phrase 'to another man' (Lev. 27:20) excludes a son from triggering the field's transfer to the priests, but not a brother?
o: Because the Torah never mentions brothers

Because a son stands in his father's place for two other halakhot (designating a Hebrew maidservant, inheriting a Hebrew slave), while a brother's only parallel role — levirate marriage — applies only when there is no son
Because brothers cannot legally redeem land
Because sons always inherit more than brothers
quiz.e: The word 'man' already includes a brother, so 'another' must exclude someone more specific — the son, who is shown elsewhere to stand more fully in his father's place than a brother does (since levirate marriage only occurs when there is no son).

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens to an ancestral field at the Jubilee if the owner's SON redeemed it (rather than the owner himself)?
o: It goes to the priests
It never returns to anyone, remaining with the Temple treasury
It returns to the father, the original owner
It is divided between the son and the priests
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that when the son redeems the field, it returns to his father (the original owner) at the Jubilee — unlike redemption by another person or relative, which sends it to the priests.

quiz.q: What is Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma to Rav Ḥisda, and how is it resolved?
o: Whether a field can be consecrated at all near the Jubilee; resolved that it cannot
Whether an unredeemed field consecrated less than two years before the Jubilee (redeemable only at full price, no discount) still transfers to the priests; resolved that it does
Whether priests can redeem their own fields; resolved that they cannot
Whether the sela-and-pundeyon payment applies to purchased fields; resolved that it does not
quiz.e: Rami bar Ḥama asks whether a field consecrated too close to the Jubilee to qualify for discounted redemption still goes to the priests if unredeemed. Rav Ḥisda concludes it does, since the relevant verse's condition is simply whether the field was fit for redemption at all, which it was.

quiz.q: In the three-way dispute over a field that was never redeemed by the time the Jubilee arrives, what does Rabbi Eliezer rule?
o: The priests take it for free, exactly like Rabbi Shimon
The priests take it but must pay the Temple treasury, exactly like Rabbi Yehuda
The priests do not enter the field at all — it remains with the Temple treasury as a 'forsaken field' until someone eventually redeems it
The field returns automatically to the original owner
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the priests never take possession of an unredeemed field on their own; it stays with the Temple treasury, termed a 'forsaken field,' potentially through multiple Jubilee cycles, until someone actually redeems it.
